summary: For ages 7–9: children classify rainforest organisms into six major groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, insects, plants) by DEFINING observable features rather than by appearance, behaviour or habitat. The heart of the learning is criterion-driven sorting using a branching yes/no key, confronting near-miss cases (bat, caiman, tree frog), and understanding that classification helps scientists organise the rainforest's overwhelming variety. Activities span drag-and-sort of organism cards/pictures with feedback, a branching key for reasoning, a reference 'meet the groups' plate, and an end assessment. Organisms are identified from pictures/cards — children do not handle real rainforest animals.
misconceptions: 'If it flies it's a bird' — bats (mammals) and insects (butterflies) also fly.
'Frogs and lizards are the same kind' — confusing amphibians (moist skin, aquatic larvae) with reptiles (dry scales).
'Big/scary animals are one group' — sorting by size or fierceness rather than features.
'Plants aren't really organisms to classify' — overlooking plants as a major living group.
'Insects are just any little creepy-crawly' — spiders (8 legs) and worms are not insects.

activities.title: Specimen-sorting bench: sort by defining feature
steps: Lay out a set of rainforest organisms — a toucan, a jaguar, a poison dart frog, a caiman, a leaf-cutter ant, an orchid, a bat, a tree fern — as cards, pictures, or draggable tiles.
Sort each organism into one of six labelled groups: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, insects, plants.
For each placement, state the DEFINING feature that justifies it aloud or in writing (e.g. 'fur and feeds milk → mammal'; 'feathers and beak → bird').
Deliberately tackle the tricky cases: place the bat, the caiman, and the tree frog and defend each choice by feature, not by what it does.
Include the plants (orchid, tree fern) as a major group, not just the animals.
activities.insight: Living things are grouped by defining body features (fur+milk, feathers+beak, dry scales, moist skin with young that usually develop in water, six legs+three body parts, makes own food), not by what they do or where they live — so a bat and a jaguar belong together even though the bat flies.

activities.title: Branching yes/no key: let the criterion decide
steps: Use a branching yes/no key that asks about one feature at a time: 'Does it make its own food (a plant)?' → 'Does it have feathers?' → 'Does it have fur / feed milk?' → 'Does it have dry scales?' → 'Does it have moist, smooth skin with no scales?' → 'Six legs and three body parts?' — each 'yes' leads to one of the six groups (an organism that answers 'no' to every question, such as a spider or worm, belongs to a different group).
Run a tricky animal (e.g. the bat) through the key: answer 'feathers? no … fur? yes … feeds milk? yes' and watch the key narrow to MAMMAL.
Run at least two more organisms (e.g. caiman, tree frog, leaf-cutter ant) through the key and record which feature answer settled the group.
Reverse the process: pick a group and name the sequence of feature answers that leads to it, checking the key is reversible.
Discuss: because each step tests a feature, the group is decided by the criterion, not by a guess.
activities.insight: A classification key makes sorting criterion-driven, reversible and checkable: each feature question narrows the possibilities until one group remains, so the answer is justified by features rather than by a lucky guess.

activities.title: Meet the six groups: feature reference
steps: Study a reference plate of the six groups, each with its defining-feature caption and an example (tap or read: jaguar → 'mammal: fur, feeds milk'; toucan → 'bird: feathers, beak'; caiman → 'reptile: dry scales'; poison dart frog → 'amphibian: moist skin, tadpoles grow in water'; ant → 'insect: six legs, three body parts'; orchid → 'plant: makes own food').
Match each defining-feature icon (feathers, fur+milk, dry scales, moist skin, six legs, makes-own-food) to its group.
Use the plate as a check BEFORE sorting (to learn the features) and AFTER sorting (to confirm a tricky call).

Name and use the technical terms — mammal, amphibian, reptile, and invertebrate (an animal with no backbone; insects are one kind, but spiders and worms are invertebrates too) — attached to each concrete feature.
activities.insight: Each major group has one or two defining features and a correct technical name; knowing these features is the reference you use to justify any sorting decision.

activities.title: Classification check: sort and justify
steps: Sort at least eight rainforest organisms into their correct groups (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, insects, plants).
For each group, state the key feature that defines it (e.g. 'mammals have fur and feed milk to their young').
Answer the diagnostic: 'A bat flies by night, a macaw flies by day; both have wings and fly — are they both birds? Put each into its group and explain WHY.'
Explain in your own words why sorting living things into groups helps scientists understand and study the huge variety of rainforest life.
Apply the rule to a NEW or tricky case: 'If you found an animal with fur that lays eggs, how would you decide its group?'
activities.insight: A learner who has met the objective sorts by observable features, states the defining feature for each group, and applies the feature-rule correctly to tricky or novel cases — not by what an animal does or where it lives.

checkQuestion: A bat flies through the rainforest at night. A macaw flies through it by day. Both have wings and both fly — so are they both birds? Put each into its animal group, and then tell me WHY you grouped them that way.
checkAnswer: No — the macaw is a bird but the bat is a mammal. You group animals by their body features, not by what they do: birds have feathers, wings and beaks and lay eggs; the bat has fur and feeds milk to its babies, which makes it a mammal even though it flies. So flying doesn't make something a bird.
